paras: The lynching of Charley Branch took place late on the night of Tuesday, December 26, 1882, near Varner Station, Arkansas, when an armed mob took Branch, a Black man, from his guards and hanged him to a telegraph pole. Branch had been arrested two days earlier, accused of ravishing and murdering a nine-year-old girl. A short Little Rock wire dispatch carried the news across the country, and several papers headlined it with approval, the Omaha Daily Bee calling it "A Deed to Applaud."

According to a Little Rock dispatch of December 26, Branch, also printed as "Charley C. Branch," was accused of ravishing and murdering "a colored girl nine years old" at Varner Station on Sunday, December 24. He was arrested, and by December 26 "intense excitement" prevailed, with threats of hanging by a mob. The girl was not named in any of the reports.

Late on Tuesday night, an "armed mob" took Branch from the guards who held him near Varner Station, on the Little Rock & Mississippi River railway. The mob hanged him to a telegraph pole. The dispatches did not name the guards, say where Branch was held, or give the size or identity of the mob.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official inquiry appears in the coverage, which ended within a week of the hanging.

The first reports, sent on December 26 before the hanging, appeared in crime roundups the next day; several ran the Branch item directly after an Arkadelphia dispatch about the suicide of former state senate secretary Lou T. Kretschmer, so that some papers placed the crime at Arkadelphia. The lynching itself reached readers through a one-sentence Little Rock dispatch printed on December 28 and 29 from Savannah and Washington to St. Paul, Wheeling and Yankton.

Every version stated the accusation as established fact, calling Branch "the negro who ravished and murdered" or "assaulted and murdered" the girl. Headlines varied from the neutral "Hanged to a Telegraph Pole" in the National Republican and the Savannah Morning News to "A NEGRO BRUTE LYNCHED" in the St. Paul Daily Globe, "A MURDERER LYNCHED" in the New-York Tribune and "A Deed to Applaud" in the Omaha Daily Bee. The Stark County Democrat in Ohio reduced the story to a single line, describing Branch as a "negro rapist of Little Rock" "launched into eternity from a telegraph pole." No Arkansas paper's own account was found, and the coverage contains no Black press reports.

The reports differ on spelling and place, giving the name as Charley, Charles or "Brauch" and the station as Varner, "Varnor," "Vernon" or "Warner"; the Little Rock dispatches consistently say Varner Station. One Washington version said Branch was arrested on December 26 itself, and the Daily Leader put the alleged crime on Tuesday, while the other reports place the alleged crime on Sunday.

reader.title: Lynching of Charley Branch
bases: An armed mob took the accused man from his guards and hanged him to a telegraph pole (A7, A9, A17).
An 'armed mob' with no lawful authority took Branch from his guards and hanged him (A7, A10, A17), in answer to an accusation that he had ravished and murdered a nine-year-old girl (A1, A9).

The arrest and threats appear in Dec. 26 dispatches from Little Rock and Arkadelphia (A1, A2), and the hanging in a Dec. 27 Little Rock dispatch carried by many papers (A7, A9, A17); all of it is wire copy, with no local or independent account.

framing.detail: The Omaha Daily Bee headed the dispatch 'A Deed to Applaud.' and the St. Paul Daily Globe 'A NEGRO BRUTE LYNCHED.'
Most papers ran the Little Rock dispatch without comment, stating the accusation as fact, under headings such as 'Hanged to a Telegraph Pole.' or in news-in-brief columns.
The New-York Tribune headed it 'A MURDERER LYNCHED.' and the Stark County Democrat called Branch a 'negro rapist' 'launched into eternity'.

conflicts.note: Spelling variants of one name; 'Brauch' is likely a typesetting or OCR error.
The Arkadelphia dateline belongs to the Kretschmer suicide item that the Branch item followed; the Little Rock dispatches name Varner Station consistently.

conflicts.note: All lynching dispatches agree the hanging was late Tuesday night; the Daily Leader's 'Tuesday' appears to be a garble.
The Dec. 25 dateline cannot be right for a report of a Tuesday-night event; all versions say 'Late Tuesday night'.
